title: What Matter Is
objective: After this level you can explain matter as anything that has mass and takes up space.
summary: Matter is anything with mass that takes up space, even air: a small room holds about 60 kg of it. Mass is how much matter there is; weight is the pull of gravity on it.

cards.headline: The air in a small bedroom has a mass of about 60 kilograms.
cards.body: You can't see it, and you walk straight through it. Yet it has mass, just like the bed. So what makes something count as matter?

cards.fact: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space.
cards.context: Those are the two tests. An ant passes them, and so do a truck, the Earth and a whole galaxy. Gases pass too, even invisible ones: if gas didn't take up space, blowing into a balloon wouldn't make it bigger. Remember Level 1? Chemistry is the study of what matter is made of and how it changes. This is its raw material.

cards.headline: Weighing a room full of air
cards.body: A liter of dry air has a mass of only about 1.2 grams. But rooms hold a lot of liters. A small bedroom, 4 meters by 5 meters with a 2.5-meter ceiling, holds 50,000 liters of air, about 60 kilograms of it. You've been sharing your room with a heavyweight all along.

cards.headline: Mass isn't weight
cards.body: Mass is how much matter something contains. Weight is the pull of gravity on that matter. Send an astronaut to the Moon, where gravity is one-sixth of Earth's, and she weighs one-sixth as much. Her mass doesn't change at all: same astronaut, same matter, lighter footsteps.
cards.callout: Mass: how much matter. Weight: how hard gravity pulls on it.

mascot.line: People mix up mass and weight all the time. Mass is the stuff; weight is gravity's pull on it.

cards.headline: Matter: measured
learned: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space
Air is matter: a small room holds about 60 kg of it
Mass is how much matter; weight is gravity's pull

questions.prompt: About how much mass does the air in a small bedroom (4 m by 5 m, 2.5 m ceiling) have?

options.label: About 60 grams
options.rationale: Far too little: each liter alone is about 1.2 grams.

questions.explanation: 50,000 liters of air at about 1.2 grams per liter comes to about 60 kilograms.

questions.prompt: An astronaut travels from Earth to the Moon. What happens to her mass?

options.label: It drops to one-sixth
options.rationale: That is her weight, which depends on gravity.

options.label: It becomes zero
options.rationale: She is still made of the same matter.

options.label: It doubles
options.rationale: Nothing adds matter to her on the trip.

questions.explanation: Mass is the amount of matter, so it stays the same. Only her weight, gravity's pull, drops to one-sixth.

questions.prompt: Level 1 said chemistry studies matter. Why does the invisible air in a room count as matter?

options.label: Air counts only when it moves as wind
options.rationale: Still air has mass and takes up space too.

options.label: It doesn't: only solids and liquids are matter
options.rationale: Gases are matter too, as a balloon shows.

options.label: Air counts only when it is cold
options.rationale: Temperature has nothing to do with it.

options.label: Air has mass and takes up space

questions.explanation: Anything with mass that takes up space is matter, which puts air squarely in chemistry's territory.
